los.text: Describe the main causes, signs and symptoms, and pathophysiology of lung cancer
los.html:
Causes/risk factors
  • Smoking (~70–80%; dose-related, pack-years; passive smoking)
  • Asbestos (synergistic with smoking; also mesothelioma)
  • Radon (2nd commonest cause in UK)
  • Air pollution
  • Occupational (arsenic, nickel, chromium, silica)
  • Previous radiotherapy
  • Pulmonary fibrosis
  • COPD
  • FHx
  • HIV.
Types
TypeFeatures
Adenocarcinoma (commonest, ~40%)Peripheral; non-smokers and women; EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS mutations (targetable)
Squamous cell (~25%)Central; smokers; cavitation; PTHrP → hypercalcaemia
Small cell (~15%)Central; strongly smoking-related; neuroendocrine; fast-growing, early metastasis; SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert–Eaton
Large cell, carcinoidCarcinoid: younger, bronchial obstruction
Pathophysiology
  • Carcinogens → stepwise mutations (TP53, KRAS, EGFR, CDKN2A) → squamous metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive.
  • Spread: local (pleura, chest wall, mediastinum), lymphatic (hilar, mediastinal), blood (brain, bone, liver, adrenals).
SymptomsPersistent cough, haemoptysis, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, fatigue, hoarseness (left recurrent laryngeal nerve), recurrent chest infections.
SignsClubbing, cachexia, supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, effusion, collapse/consolidation signs.
Local complicationsSVC obstruction (facial swelling, distended neck veins, headache), Pancoast tumour (apex: shoulder/arm pain, Horner's syndrome, T1 wasting), phrenic nerve palsy, pericardial effusion.
ParaneoplasticSIADH, Cushing's (SCLC), hypercalcaemia (SCC), Lambert–Eaton, hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (adenocarcinoma), cerebellar degeneration.
  • NICE: urgent CXR within 2 weeks if ≥40 with ≥2 symptoms (or 1 if smoker) such as cough
  • fatigue
  • breathlessness
  • chest pain
  • weight loss
  • appetite loss
  • 2WW if CXR suggests cancer or unexplained haemoptysis ≥40.

los.text: Describe the diagnosis, prognosis and principles of treatment / management of lung cancer
los.html:
Diagnosis
  • CXR
  • → contrast CT chest/abdomen (to adrenals)
  • → tissue diagnosis: bronchoscopy with EBUS-TBNA (samples mediastinal nodes = diagnosis + staging), CT-guided biopsy (peripheral), pleural aspiration/biopsy, node/metastasis biopsy.
  • PET-CT for staging in those for radical treatment
  • MRI brain
  • Bone scan.
  • Molecular testing (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS G12C, BRAF, PD-L1).
  • Lung function (FEV1, TLCO) and performance status (WHO/ECOG 0–4) determine fitness.
StagingTNM (8th edition) for NSCLC; SCLC: limited vs extensive.
Prognosis
  • Overall poor (~10–15% 5-year survival UK) because most present late
  • Stage I ~60–80% 5-year survival
  • SCLC extensive median ~1 year.
  • Better with early detection (targeted lung health checks/screening with low-dose CT for high-risk smokers, rolling out nationally) and targeted therapies.
Treatment principles (MDT)
  • NSCLC early stage (I–II): surgical resection (lobectomy + lymph node sampling) if fit; SABR (stereotactic ablative radiotherapy) if unfit; adjuvant chemo/immunotherapy/osimertinib (EGFR).
  • Stage III: concurrent chemoradiotherapy + durvalumab consolidation, or surgery in selected cases.
  • Stage IV: targeted therapy if driver mutation (EGFR: osimertinib; ALK: alectinib/lorlatinib), otherwise immunotherapy (pembrolizumab: PD-1 inhibitor) ± platinum chemotherapy; palliative RT.
  • SCLC: platinum + etoposide chemotherapy (+ immunotherapy in extensive) ± thoracic RT, prophylactic cranial irradiation; very chemosensitive initially but relapses.
Supportive/palliative
  • SVC stenting + steroids
  • Pleural drainage/indwelling catheter
  • Endobronchial stenting
  • Symptom control (opioids for breathlessness/pain)
  • Smoking cessation
  • Lung cancer nurse specialist
  • Early palliative care referral (improves quality of life and possibly survival).

los.text: Describe the key principles and practices of palliative care in managing end-of-life patients
los.html:
Palliative care (WHO)
  • Approach improving the quality of life of patients and families facing life-threatening illness, through prevention and relief of suffering by early identification, assessment and treatment of pain and other physical, psychosocial and spiritual problems.
  • Affirms life, regards dying as normal, neither hastens nor postpones death.
Key principles
  • Holistic
  • Patient- and family-centred
  • MDT (GP, district nurses, specialist palliative care, hospice, chaplaincy, social work)
  • Early integration alongside active treatment
  • Open communication
  • Respect for preferences
  • Bereavement support.
Identifying end of lifeSurprise question ("Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next year?"), SPICT tool, Gold Standards Framework register.
Advance care planning
  • Preferences and priorities (preferred place of care/death)
  • Advance decision to refuse treatment
  • Lasting power of attorney
  • DNACPR decisions (ReSPECT form)
  • Treatment escalation plans.
Symptom managementPain (WHO ladder; opioids; adjuvants), breathlessness (opioids, fan, positioning), nausea (cause-specific antiemetics), constipation (laxatives with opioids), agitation/delirium, secretions, mouth care, anxiety/depression.
Last days of life
  • Recognise dying (bed-bound, ↓ intake, ↓ consciousness)
  • Stop non-essential drugs/observations
  • Anticipatory ("just in case") medications SC: opioid (pain/breathlessness), midazolam (agitation/anxiety), antiemetic (levomepromazine/haloperidol), anti-secretory (glycopyrronium/hyoscine butylbromide)
  • Syringe driver
  • Hydration discussed individually
  • Care for family
  • Verification and certification of death.
  • Wales: "Care Decisions for the Last Days of Life" guidance.
